name: Freya Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and lead the morning call queue at the contact centre. My two-year college diploma helped me get here, but most of what I know came from tracing booking errors with customers still on the line. I’m one of the strongest agents, yet the lead rate is low. I occasionally use AI to sort a long chat history after another lead showed me how; I check every account detail myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Omar drives deliveries, and our two children are in school. We have a mortgage and less than one month of expenses saved. There are few similar jobs near us. I like handing a caller a clear answer; I hate guessing how many paid hours next month’s rota will carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the morning team AI Plateau leaves most customer work with us. A quick chat summary is useful only after somebody checks the booking and the payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I would keep my lead hours, although low pay already leaves Omar and me very little room. A tool that saves minutes will not fill our savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep tracing the complicated bookings and use the chat summary tool on one long case a week, checking it against the account. In the first year of this small change, I’d put the cost of one weekly takeaway into our mortgage buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the queue, uneasy about the bank balance. A faster summary does not make my next mortgage payment smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a summary get wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the summary said a customer missed a flight, but the booking showed the airline cancelled it. I changed the note before the next agent saw it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you save that amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar (my partner) and I would cook on Friday instead of ordering food. The children keep their school activities; that small saving is one we can sustain.

I’d use **chat summaries** only after verifying them.
think: I think my **lead hours** probably remain with most customer calls still handled here.
I still see our **thin savings** as a problem.
do: Keep handling **complicated bookings** and verify one AI summary weekly.
Cook instead of the **weekly takeaway** and transfer its cost into the mortgage buffer.

fieldNote: Her **occasional AI use** includes checking the account record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team Steady Disruption will strip out the easy bookings and leave us with missed payments and upset callers. I would ask our manager for a paid rota, not a count of messages handled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could supervise the difficult queue if the company still pays for that work. But even a few lost shifts would put our mortgage under strain, and there are few contact centres close enough for the school run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep a record of bookings the tool gets wrong and test its summaries against the account with another lead. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid complaints role only if its written weekly hours and wage cover the mortgage after travel and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful and a little anxious. I can learn a proven tool, but I cannot budget with an imaginary rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your record show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the cases that come back after an automated answer, including the time an agent spends repairing them. That tells us whether the shorter queue really needs fewer paid people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What costs matter in another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar (my partner) has an early delivery route some weeks. I would price the extra childcare and bus fare before accepting any complaints shift.

say: I’d ask for **paid rota hours** as simple bookings move.
I’d show **returned cases** the tool got wrong.
think: I think I might lead the **difficult queue** if the company keeps paying for it.
I fear **lost shifts** would strain our mortgage.
do: Record **wrong bookings** and test summaries with another lead in 2026.
Seek **posted paid complaints work** only with written weekly wages and hours covering mortgage after travel and childcare.

fieldNote: She distinguishes **paid shifts** from message volume.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 could answer nearly every call and decide which booking is wrong. I would ask management for the dates our paid morning shifts could change, before anyone starts selling us a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead skill buys little protection if thinking AI is cheaper in 2028. Robots around 2031 are a separate later problem; my mortgage would already need paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d cancel plans for a second car and keep the deposit in our mortgage reserve. In the first year after 2028, I’d take a posted paid school-office job only if the written weekly wage, hours and school-run schedule work after travel; if it requires an office course, I’d take it only when funded on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I know how to fix an account, but I cannot fix a vanished wage with less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the car plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have Omar (my partner) and me use the bus and share the car we have rather than make another payment. His delivery vehicle belongs to work, so I would not count it as family transport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make office training worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the school for the actual office vacancy and hours. I would not pay for a general certificate while waiting for a job that might not exist.

say: I’d ask management for **written shift dates** before anyone starts pitching courses to my team.
I’d say **2028 AGI** reaches calls before robots.
think: I think my **lead skill** may not protect the wage.
I know **2031 robots** arrive after our first mortgage risk.
do: Cancel the **second-car plan** and keep the deposit in 2026.
Move after 2028 to **posted school-office work** only with written weekly pay and hours covering mortgage after travel, and workable school runs.
Take **funded paid-time office training** only if that vacancy requires it.
S2.quote: I know how to fix an account, but I cannot fix a vanished wage with less than a month saved.
fieldNote: She does not count Omar’s **work vehicle** as family transport.
The **car deposit** becomes a mortgage reserve.
Office training needs a **real vacancy** and funded paid time.

steps.text: Cancel the second-car plan and preserve its deposit for mortgage costs
Take posted school-office job only with written after-cost wage, hours and workable school runs
Take funded office course on paid time only if posted school vacancy requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2031 gives us time to demand real transition hours, not just login details for a course. I would ask whether the centre has a paid booking-dispute role posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years may let me use my booking knowledge in dispute review. I also know full thinking AI could read that evidence by 2031, so a new title alone is no shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d shadow the paid dispute reviewer for two shifts if the manager allows it on my rota, then take the required course only if a posted paid reviewer vacancy exists and the employer funds the time. In the first year after 2031, I’d move only with a signed offer showing weekly hours and a wage covering our mortgage after travel and childcare; otherwise I’d keep any paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there is enough time to see the real job. I want the vacancy before I buy the dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you observe while shadowing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would follow one booking from the first complaint through the refund decision and ask who can correct the account. If the reviewer only forwards forms, I would stay on calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Omar check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar (my partner) would check the school pickup on a reviewer rota with me. A late shift might require paid childcare even if the hourly rate rises.

say: I’d ask for **paid transition hours** and a posted review role.
I’d question whether a **new title** changes the work.
think: I think I could use my **booking knowledge** in a paid dispute-review post.
I know **2031 AGI** could also read disputes.
do: Shadow **dispute review** for two paid rota shifts if allowed; keep calls if no suitable offer appears.
Take the **required reviewer course** only for a posted paid vacancy with employer-funded paid study time.
Move after 2031 only with **signed weekly wages/hours** covering mortgage after travel and childcare, and workable pickup.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to inspect the job.
S3.quote: I want the vacancy before I buy the dream.
fieldNote: She wants to see **correction authority** in dispute review.
Training requires **posted paid work** and employer-funded time.
A signed offer must cover **childcare and travel**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives our centre a decade to show how many paid agents it will need each year. I would ask the leads to take that question together to management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can build a slightly better reserve while keeping a wage, but full thinking AI may still take calls in 2036. Robots around 2039 do not extend the date for my queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading morning calls and arrange an automatic small transfer after each payday. In the first year after 2036, if my hours fall, I’d seek a posted paid account-support role only with a signed offer whose weekly wage and hours cover mortgage, travel and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious rather than calm. Ten years gives my partner Omar and me more paydays, but it does not make this month’s mortgage wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would leads ask together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask each lead to sign the same request for yearly paid-hours forecasts. That is harder to brush off as one person worrying about her own shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not move the children for a rumoured opening. Omar (my partner) and I would consider it only with a signed job offer and a school journey we can both manage.

I’d tell colleagues **2036 thinking AI** reaches calls before robots.
think: I think I could **save more** over ten years if my paid morning hours remain.
I know **2036 AGI** still threatens my queue.
do: Join **other leads’ yearly-hours request**, keep morning calls and transfer a little from each payday to savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because calls could vanish while our mortgage still arrives every month. I would need early written notice, enough paid hours to bridge to a posted job, and time to learn a required new role while I am still earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Please ask whether a new job gives a parent the same usable week, not just a higher hourly rate. Omar (my partner) cannot cover both school runs when his delivery route changes.

headlineQuote: Please ask whether a new job gives a parent the same usable week, not just a higher hourly rate.
portrait: At **43**, Freya leads morning contact-centre calls after a two-year diploma and years of customer work.
Her **low lead wage** supports two schoolchildren and a mortgage alongside Omar’s delivery earnings.
With **under one month saved**, she fears losing paid hours before finding another local job.
She uses **AI occasionally** for chat histories but verifies account details herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove paid call hours before she can secure another mortgage-paying role.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, continued paid hours and paid training tied to a posted job would help.
